newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran says Moslems hold new political rally at haj.
newsitem.headline: Iran says Moslems hold new political rally at haj.

text.p: A large crowd of Moslems held another rally against the United States and Israel at the haj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, defying a Saudi ban, Iranian state media said.
Tehran radio said pilgrims chanted "Death to Israel" and "Death to America" near Mount Arafat, outside the city of Mecca -- site of Islam's holiest shrine.
There was no independent confirmation of the report or reaction from Saudi Arabia.

Iran's news agency IRNA said pilgrims from Iran and other countries including Kuwait, Egypt, Algeria, Afghanistan, Libya, Bosnia, France, Germany and the Netherlands attended the rally at an Iranian pilgrimage tent compound.

Iran earlier said pilgrims had held their first "disavowal of infidels" rally on Monday in Mecca despite the Saudi ban against all political activities during haj. There was no word from Saudi Arabia on the reported demonstration.

Iran has said some 72,000 Iranians were performing haj this year. Tehran said there were no casualties among its pilgrims in a fire which ripped through a tent compound on Tuesday, killing 217 people and injuring some 1,300.

Tense relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran usually take a turn for the worse over the staging of the rally during the annual haj, which reached its climax on Wednesday with two million Moslems attending.
Radical Shi'ite Iran says Moslems should air political grievances during haj, mainly through rallies to denounce Israel and the United States as enemies of Islam.
Conservative Sunni Saudi Arabia says the pilgrimage is purely religious and should not be politicised.

The row between the Gulf's two richest oil states has resurfaced at every haj since 1987, when 402 people, mostly Iranians, died in clashes with Saudi security forces at an Iranian-led rally. Iran boycotted haj for three years.

Saudi Arabia had said it would deal harshly with violators of the ban on political activity during haj. To avoid confrontation with Saudi security, Iranian pilgrims in recent years staged low-key rallies within Iran's haj compounds and Saudi forces did not interfere.
Iran is trying to improve relations with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Arab states and its officials and state media had in the run up to haj been using softer tones towards the kingdom.
